transcript.answer: As a dispatcher, I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, meaning I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. transcript.answer: I worry about closures coming into force while our drones are already in the air, especially since zones and sudden closures can be announced or amended during the day. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and relay station reports can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and the service itself runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours and occasionally crashes.

transcript.question: When a closure comes into force while one of your drones is already in the air, what do you do today?

transcript.answer: I worry because the service runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours, while drones are flying, and it occasionally crashes. We accept a few minutes of interruption when this happens.

While a dispatcher is planning with a drone, the service must show whether that drone is already on another of the company's flights at an overlapping time.
When two users change the same flight, drone or pad at the same time, the service must not silently discard either change. It must apply one and tell the other user that their change was not applied.
When the same report from a drone or relay station arrives more than once, the service must count it once.

When a report arrives after a newer report from the same drone, the service must keep the older one in the flight's record at its original time. It must not let it overwrite the drone's current position, battery or status.
For every flight in the air, the service must show the dispatcher the time of the drone's last report. It must never present the last known position or battery as current without that time.
When no report has arrived from a drone in the air for longer than a period the company sets, the service must alert that company's dispatchers that the drone is silent.
When a drone's reported battery is below what the flight plan expected at that point by more than a margin the company sets, the service must alert that company's dispatchers.

Every instruction the service sends to a drone or to charging equipment must be built so that receiving it twice has the same effect as receiving it once. A repeated send must be the same instruction with the same identity, never a new one.
The service must show an instruction as unconfirmed until a report shows it took effect, and must never show it as done merely because it was sent.
When an instruction stays unconfirmed for longer than a set time, the service must tell the user who issued it.
The service must work on a single server and must not depend on a second server being available.

Everything the service has confirmed to a user must still be there unchanged after the server is restarted or crashes. This includes drones, pads, upkeep records, flights, sign-offs, call-offs, closures and their amendments, alerts, and instructions sent.
After a planned restart or a crash, the service must be working again without anyone re-entering data, within a few minutes. The exact limit is not given in the interviews and must be agreed.
When the service comes back after an interruption, it must apply any closure whose start time passed while it was down, and must raise the alerts of DR-20 and DR-21 that it would have raised.
When the service comes back after an interruption, it must accept reports that were delayed during it and record them at the time they were made, following DR-38 and DR-39.

When the service comes back after an interruption, instructions that were unconfirmed when it stopped must still be shown as unconfirmed. If resent, they must be resent as the same instruction under DR-43.

The service must serve several companies at once, each with a few hundred drones of several models and manufacturers and a few dozen charging pads, with several dispatchers per company planning at the same time.
